lesson.title: Why 'was £80, now £40' works: price anchoring
body: The first number we see sets a reference point, and we judge everything after it against that. Marketers call this anchoring. A crossed-out 'was' price makes the 'now' price feel like a win, even if you'd never have paid the higher one.
Black Friday runs on it. You'll also see it in three-tier pricing, where a pricey 'premium' option makes the middle one look sensible, and in 'worth £200' bundles.

Used honestly, anchoring helps customers understand value. Used badly it backfires: UK rules on misleading prices mean a 'was' price should be one the item was genuinely sold at. As a shopper, ignore the anchor and compare the actual price elsewhere.
lesson.takeaway: Customers judge a price against the first number they see, so choose that number carefully and keep it honest.

m365.title: Keep important files on your device with OneDrive
m365.what: Files On-Demand only shows most OneDrive and SharePoint files as online until you open them. If Microsoft 365 goes down, as it did on 12–13 November, you can't open them. Marking key folders 'Always keep on this device' keeps a full local copy that still syncs when the service is back.
try: On Windows, open File Explorer and go to your OneDrive folder (or a SharePoint library you've synced).
Right-click the folder you'd need during an outage, e.g. current projects, and choose 'Always keep on this device'.
Wait for the status icon to turn into a solid green circle with a white tick. That means the files are stored locally.
Save desktop copies of Word, Excel and PowerPoint files you use every day. They open offline and changes sync later.
Don't do this for huge folders on a small drive. To reverse it, right-click and choose 'Free up space'.

explainer.story: Why Microsoft 365 went down for almost a day
bullets: On 12 November Outlook and Exchange Online stopped working worldwide for nearly 24 hours, and Teams and Copilot were partly hit. Microsoft confirmed full recovery at about 4pm UK time on 13 November.

Microsoft says a bug added in July to its networking gateway servers sat unnoticed for over three months. Lab load tests didn't catch it because they used less powerful hardware than the live servers.

Extra traffic from a Teams failover, plus about 14% of servers already offline, triggered the bug. More than 80% of servers stopped responding, and safeguards between regions also failed. Microsoft has added capacity, improved monitoring and added safeguards.
explainer.why: Much of UK work depends on Microsoft 365. One hidden bug can still take everything down, so it's worth having an offline plan.

term.meaning: When one part of a system fails, its work moves to other parts. They get overloaded and fail too, so a small fault spreads into a big outage.
term.example: In this month's Microsoft 365 outage, traffic from failing servers was redirected to others, which then also failed. At the worst point, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

money.tip: The price cap limits unit rates and standing charges, not your total bill. What you pay still depends on how much you use. Submitting a meter reading before a price change means you're billed at the right rate for energy already used.
